questions.explanation_text: For the equilibrium $P_{2}(g)+Q_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2PQ(g)$ $K_{c}=\frac{[PQ]^{2}}{[P_{2}][Q_{2}]}$ Since $[X]=n_{X}/V$ , the volume cancels: $K_{c}=\frac{(n_{PQ}/V)^{2}}{(n_{P_{2}}/V)(n_{Q_{2}}/V)}=\frac{n_{PQ}^{2}}{n_{P_{2}}n_{Q_{2}}}$ 1) Find $K_{c}$ from the given equilibrium Initially at equilibrium: $n_{P_{2}}=2,n_{Q_{2}}=2,n_{PQ}=2$ $K_{c}=\frac{2^{2}}{2 \cdot 2}=1$ 2) After adding 1 mol each of $P_{2},Q_{2}$ Immediately after addition: $n_{P_{2}}=3,n_{Q_{2}}=3,n_{PQ}=2$ Let the reaction proceed forward by extent $x$ : $n_{P_{2}}=3-x,n_{Q_{2}}=3-x,n_{PQ}=2+2x$ Apply $K_{c}=1$ : $1=\frac{(2+2x)^{2}}{(3-x)(3-x)}=\frac{(2+2x)^{2}}{(3-x)^{2}}$ $(2+2x)^{2}=(3-x)^{2} \Rightarrow 2+2x=3-x \Rightarrow 3x=1 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{3}$ So, $n_{P_{2}}=3-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$ $n_{Q_{2}}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$ $n_{PQ}=2+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$ Answer: Option B $(2.67,2.67,2.67)$ .
questions.explanation_html:
For the equilibrium

$P_{2}(g)+Q_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2PQ(g)$

$K_{c}=\frac{[PQ]^{2}}{[P_{2}][Q_{2}]}$

Since $[X]=n_{X}/V$ , the volume cancels:

$K_{c}=\frac{(n_{PQ}/V)^{2}}{(n_{P_{2}}/V)(n_{Q_{2}}/V)}=\frac{n_{PQ}^{2}}{n_{P_{2}}n_{Q_{2}}}$

1) Find $K_{c}$ from the given equilibrium

Initially at equilibrium: $n_{P_{2}}=2,n_{Q_{2}}=2,n_{PQ}=2$

$K_{c}=\frac{2^{2}}{2 \cdot 2}=1$

2) After adding 1 mol each of $P_{2},Q_{2}$

Immediately after addition: $n_{P_{2}}=3,n_{Q_{2}}=3,n_{PQ}=2$

Let the reaction proceed forward by extent $x$ :

$n_{P_{2}}=3-x,n_{Q_{2}}=3-x,n_{PQ}=2+2x$

Apply $K_{c}=1$ :

$1=\frac{(2+2x)^{2}}{(3-x)(3-x)}=\frac{(2+2x)^{2}}{(3-x)^{2}}$

$(2+2x)^{2}=(3-x)^{2} \Rightarrow 2+2x=3-x \Rightarrow 3x=1 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{3}$

So,

$n_{P_{2}}=3-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$

$n_{Q_{2}}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$

$n_{PQ}=2+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{8}{3}=2.67$

Answer: Option B $(2.67,2.67,2.67)$ .

questions.explanation_text: For the reaction $A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g)+C(g)$ initial amount of $A=a$ . At equilibrium, amount of $A$ left $=a-x$ . So, amount of $A$ dissociated $=x$ . Hence at equilibrium: $A=a-x$ $B=x$ $C=x$ Now total moles at equilibrium: $(a-x)+x+x=a+x$ Since total pressure is $p$ , the partial pressures are: $P_{A}=\frac{a-x}{a+x}p$ $P_{B}=\frac{x}{a+x}p$ $P_{C}=\frac{x}{a+x}p$ Now, $K_{p}=\frac{P_{B} \cdot P_{C}}{P_{A}}$ Substitute the values: $K_{p}=\frac{(\frac{x}{a+x}p)(\frac{x}{a+x}p)}{(\frac{a-x}{a+x}p)}$ Simplifying, $K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}p^{2}}{(a+x)^{2}} \cdot \frac{a+x}{(a-x)p}$ $K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}p}{(a+x)(a-x)}$ Using $(a+x)(a-x)=a^{2}-x^{2}$ we get $K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}-x^{2}}p$ So the correct expression is: $K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}-x^{2}} \times p$ Therefore, the correct option is: $\text{Option B}$

For the reaction

$A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g)+C(g)$

initial amount of $A=a$ .

At equilibrium, amount of $A$ left $=a-x$ .

So, amount of $A$ dissociated $=x$ .

Hence at equilibrium:

  • $A=a-x$

  • $B=x$

  • $C=x$

Now total moles at equilibrium:

$(a-x)+x+x=a+x$

Since total pressure is $p$ , the partial pressures are:

$P_{A}=\frac{a-x}{a+x}p$

$P_{B}=\frac{x}{a+x}p$

$P_{C}=\frac{x}{a+x}p$

Now,

$K_{p}=\frac{P_{B} \cdot P_{C}}{P_{A}}$

Substitute the values:

$K_{p}=\frac{(\frac{x}{a+x}p)(\frac{x}{a+x}p)}{(\frac{a-x}{a+x}p)}$

Simplifying,

$K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}p^{2}}{(a+x)^{2}} \cdot \frac{a+x}{(a-x)p}$

$K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}p}{(a+x)(a-x)}$

Using

$(a+x)(a-x)=a^{2}-x^{2}$

we get

$K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}-x^{2}}p$

So the correct expression is:

$K_{p}=\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}-x^{2}} \times p$

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option B}$

questions.explanation_text: For any gaseous reaction, the relationship between equilibrium constants is $K_{p}=K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n_{g}}$ where $\Delta n_{g}=$ (moles of gaseous products) $-$ (moles of gaseous reactants). For the given reaction $xA(g) \rightleftharpoons yB(g),$ we have $\Delta n_{g}=y-x.$ For reaction (i) : $K_{p}>K_{C}$ Since $K_{p}>K_{c}$ , using $K_{p}=K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n_{g}}$ , $\Delta n_{g}$ must be positive. So the number of moles of gaseous products is more than that of reactants. $\begin{aligned} & \Delta n_{g}>0 \\ & y-x>0 \\ & 85.87=2.586(0.0821 \times 400)^{y-x} \end{aligned}$ Here $R=0.0821Latmmol^{-1}K^{-1}$ and $T=400K$ , so $RT=0.0821 \times 400$ . From the equation $85.87=2.586(0.0821 \times 400)^{y-x},$ we get Solving $y-x≃1$ This means the products have one mole more than the reactants. So $y-x=1 \Rightarrow y=x+1.$ Taking the simplest whole numbers, we can choose $x=1$ and $y=2$ for case (i). For reaction (ii) : $K_{p}<K_{c}$ Since $K_{p}<K_{c}$ , using $K_{p}=K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n_{g}}$ , $\Delta n_{g}$ must be negative. So the number of moles of gaseous products is less than that of reactants. $y-x<0.$ Using the same relation, $K_{p}=K_{c}(RT)^{y-x},$ we write for reaction (ii) $0.862=28.62(0.0821 \times 400)^{y-x}$ Solving this, we find $y-x≃-1$ So the reactants have one mole more than the products: $y-x=-1 \Rightarrow x=y+1.$ Taking the simplest whole numbers, we can choose $x=2$ and $y=1$ for case (ii).

For the reaction

we have to find the magnitude of standard free energy change, that is, $|\Delta G^{\circ}|$ .

We use the relation

So first, let us calculate $K_{p}$ .

1. Take 1 mole of $N_{2}O_{5}$ initially

Given that $N_{2}O_{5}$ is $50%$ dissociated.

If $2$ moles of $N_{2}O_{5}$ dissociate, then:

  • $2$ moles of $N_{2}O_{4}$ are formed

  • $1$ mole of $O_{2}$ is formed

Therefore, if $0.5$ mole of $N_{2}O_{5}$ dissociates:

  • $N_{2}O_{4}$ formed $=0.5$ mole

  • $O_{2}$ formed $=0.25$ mole

So at equilibrium:

$n(N_{2}O_{5})=1-0.5=0.5$

$n(N_{2}O_{4})=0.5$

$n(O_{2})=0.25$

Total moles at equilibrium:

$n_{\text{total}}=0.5+0.5+0.25=1.25$

2. Calculate mole fractions

$y_{N_{2}O_{5}}=\frac{0.5}{1.25}=0.4$

$y_{N_{2}O_{4}}=\frac{0.5}{1.25}=0.4$

$y_{O_{2}}=\frac{0.25}{1.25}=0.2$

Given total pressure $P=2$ atm.

Hence partial pressures are:

$P_{N_{2}O_{5}}=0.4 \times 2=0.8\text{atm}$

$P_{N_{2}O_{4}}=0.4 \times 2=0.8\text{atm}$

$P_{O_{2}}=0.2 \times 2=0.4\text{atm}$

For the reaction

$2N_{2}O_{5}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2N_{2}O_{4}(g)+O_{2}(g)$

Substitute the values:

$K_{p}=\frac{(0.8)^{2}(0.4)}{(0.8)^{2}}=0.4$

$K_{p}=0.4$

Temperature:

$T=50+273=323\text{K}$

Now,

$0.4=\frac{2}{5}$

Therefore,

$ln(0.4)=2.303 \times (-0.40)=-0.9212$

Now,

$\Delta G^{\circ}=-8.314 \times 323 \times (-0.9212)$

$\Delta G^{\circ} \approx 2472\text{J mol}^{-1}$

So the magnitude is

$x=2472\text{J mol}^{-1}$

Final Answer:

$2472$

According to the rule for equilibrium constants: if the coefficients of a balanced chemical equation are multiplied by $n$ , then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^{n}$ if the coefficients are divided by $n$ , then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^{1/n}$ So here, $K^{'}=K^{1/3}$ Therefore, $K^{'}=(2.7 \times 10^{-5})^{1/3}$ Now calculate: $2.7=(0.3)^{3} \times 100$ But it is easier to check directly: $(3 \times 10^{-2})^{3}=27 \times 10^{-6}=2.7 \times 10^{-5}$ So, $(2.7 \times 10^{-5})^{1/3}=3 \times 10^{-2}$ Hence, the correct answer is: $3 \times 10^{-2}$ So, Option D is correct.

questions.explanation_text: Given reaction: $X_{2}(g)+Y_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2Z(g)$ 1) Find $K_{c}$ from the first equilibrium At equilibrium in a $1L$ flask: $[X_{2}]=3,[Y_{2}]=3,[Z]=9$ $K_{c}=\frac{[Z]^{2}}{[X_{2}][Y_{2}]}=\frac{9^{2}}{3 \times 3}=\frac{81}{9}=9$ 2) After adding $10$ mol of $Z$ New moles immediately (before shift): $X_{2}=3,Y_{2}=3,Z=9+10=19$ Since $Z$ is added, equilibrium shifts left. Let the backward reaction proceed by $x$ moles: $X_{2}$ increases by $x$ $Y_{2}$ increases by $x$ $Z$ decreases by $2x$ So at new equilibrium: $[X_{2}]=3+x,[Y_{2}]=3+x,[Z]=19-2x$ 3) Apply equilibrium constant again $K_{c}=\frac{(19-2x)^{2}}{(3+x)(3+x)}=9$ $(19-2x)^{2}=9(3+x)^{2}$ Taking positive square root (concentrations are positive): $19-2x=3(3+x)=9+3x$ $19-9=3x+2x$ $10=5x \Rightarrow x=2$ Hence, $\text{New moles of}Z=19-2(2)=19-4=15$ Nearest integer = $15$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given reaction:

$K_{c}=\frac{[Z]^{2}}{[X_{2}][Y_{2}]}=\frac{9^{2}}{3 \times 3}=\frac{81}{9}=9$

2) After adding $10$ mol of $Z$

New moles immediately (before shift):

$X_{2}=3,Y_{2}=3,Z=9+10=19$

Since $Z$ is added, equilibrium shifts left. Let the backward reaction proceed by $x$ moles:

  • $X_{2}$ increases by $x$

  • $Y_{2}$ increases by $x$

  • $Z$ decreases by $2x$

So at new equilibrium:

$[X_{2}]=3+x,[Y_{2}]=3+x,[Z]=19-2x$

3) Apply equilibrium constant again

$K_{c}=\frac{(19-2x)^{2}}{(3+x)(3+x)}=9$

$(19-2x)^{2}=9(3+x)^{2}$

Taking positive square root (concentrations are positive):

$19-2x=3(3+x)=9+3x$

$19-9=3x+2x$

$10=5x \Rightarrow x=2$

Hence,

$\text{New moles of}Z=19-2(2)=19-4=15$

Nearest integer = $15$ .

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze both statements: Statement I: "A catalyst cannot alter the equilibrium constant ( $K_{c}$ ) of the reaction, temperature remaining constant." A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, allowing the system to reach equilibrium faster. However, it does not change the energy difference between reactants and products (i.e., the Gibbs free energy change), which directly determines the equilibrium constant. Therefore, this statement is true. Statement II: "A homogenous catalyst can change the equilibrium composition of a system, temperature remaining constant." A homogeneous catalyst acts in the same phase as the reactants and, like any catalyst, it only helps the reaction reach equilibrium more quickly. It does not alter the equilibrium position, meaning the relative concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium remain unchanged if the temperature is constant. Thus, this statement is false. In summary: Statement I is true. Statement II is false. The correct answer is: Option A.

Partial Pressures The total pressure $P_{\text{total}}$ is given by: $P_{X_{2}Y}=\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$ $P_{X_{2}}=\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$ $P_{Y_{2}}=\frac{x/2}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$ Equilibrium Constant Expression The equilibrium constant $K_{p}$ can be written in terms of partial pressures: $K_{p}=\frac{(\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P) \cdot (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P)^{1/2}}{\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P}$ Simplifying the expression, considering $x$ to be very small, results in: $K_{p}=(\frac{x}{1-x})(\frac{x}{2(1+\frac{x}{2})})^{1/2} \cdot P^{\frac{1}{2}}$ For small $x$ , $(1-x) \approx 1$ , thus: $K_{p}=\frac{x^{3/2}}{\frac{1}{3}} \cdot P^{\frac{1}{2}}$ $x^{3/2}=\frac{K_{p} \cdot 2^{1/2}}{P^{1/2}}$ Finally, by cubing both sides: $x^{3}=\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P}$ $x=(\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P})^{1/3}$ Thus, the degree of dissociation $x$ relates to $K_{p}$ by the equation: $x=(\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P})^{1/3}$

To determine the relationship between the degree of dissociation ( $x$ ) of $X_{2}Y(g)$ and its equilibrium constant $K_{p}$ , let's analyze the reaction:

$X_{2}Y(g) \rightleftharpoons X_{2}(g)+\frac{1}{2}Y_{2}(g)$

Initial and Change in Moles

Initially, we start with 1 mole of $X_{2}Y$ .

At equilibrium:

$X_{2}Y$ is $(1-x)$ moles.

$X_{2}$ is $x$ moles.

$\frac{1}{2}Y_{2}$ is $\frac{x}{2}$ moles.

Partial Pressures

The total pressure $P_{\text{total}}$ is given by:

$P_{X_{2}Y}=\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$

$P_{X_{2}}=\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$

$P_{Y_{2}}=\frac{x/2}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \times P$

Equilibrium Constant Expression

The equilibrium constant $K_{p}$ can be written in terms of partial pressures:

$K_{p}=\frac{(\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P) \cdot (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P)^{1/2}}{\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}} \cdot P}$

Simplifying the expression, considering $x$ to be very small, results in:

$K_{p}=(\frac{x}{1-x})(\frac{x}{2(1+\frac{x}{2})})^{1/2} \cdot P^{\frac{1}{2}}$

For small $x$ , $(1-x) \approx 1$ , thus:

$K_{p}=\frac{x^{3/2}}{\frac{1}{3}} \cdot P^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$x^{3/2}=\frac{K_{p} \cdot 2^{1/2}}{P^{1/2}}$

Finally, by cubing both sides:

$x^{3}=\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P}$

$x=(\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P})^{1/3}$

Thus, the degree of dissociation $x$ relates to $K_{p}$ by the equation:

$x=(\frac{2 \cdot K_{p}^{2}}{P})^{1/3}$

questions.explanation_text: When xenon gas, an inert gas, is added to the equilibrium system $PCl_{5}(g)⇋PCl_{3}(g)+Cl_{2}(g)$ at a constant temperature and pressure, it affects the equilibrium according to Le Chatelier's principle. The addition of an inert gas at constant pressure effectively increases the volume of the system, reducing the concentration of the gases involved. Since the system is at constant pressure, adding an inert gas increases the total volume, which favors the side of the reaction with more moles of gas. In this reaction, there are two moles of gas on the right side ( $PCl_{3}$ and $Cl_{2}$ ) compared to one mole on the left ( $PCl_{5}$ ). Thus, the equilibrium will shift toward the right to increase the number of moles and counteract the change, decreasing the concentration of $PCl_{5}$ and increasing the concentrations of $PCl_{3}$ and $Cl_{2}$ . However, due to the increase in overall volume, the individual concentrations of all species $([PCl_{5}],[PCl_{3}],[Cl_{2}])$ will decrease as a result of more space being available for the same amount of gas particles.

questions.explanation_text: To solve this problem, we need to understand the relationship between the equilibrium constant in terms of pressure, $K_{P}$ , and the equilibrium constant in terms of concentration, $K_{C}$ . questions.explanation_text: (A) Equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature. This statement is true. In a closed system, there is no exchange of matter with the surroundings. This allows the reaction to reach equilibrium at a constant temperature. (B) Both the opposing processes occur at the same rate. This statement is true. At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, meaning the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. (C) When equilibrium is attained at a given temperature, the value of all its parameters became equal. This statement is false. When a system reaches equilibrium, it doesn't mean that the values of all parameters (such as the concentrations of reactants and products) are equal. It means that these values are constant, i.e., they are not changing with time because the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal. (D) For dissolution of solids in liquids, the solubility is constant at a given temperature. This statement is true. The solubility of a solid in a liquid (in a saturated solution) is indeed constant at a given temperature and pressure. Therefore, there are 3 correct statements: (A), (B), and (D).

At 1990 K and 1 atm pressure, there are equal number of Cl 2 , molecules and Cl atoms in the
reaction mixture. The value of K p for the reaction Cl 2 (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ 2Cl (g) under the above conditions

questions.question_html:
At 1990 K and 1 atm pressure, there are equal number of Cl2, molecules and Cl atoms in the reaction mixture. The value of Kp for the reaction Cl2 (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ 2Cl(g) under the above conditions is x $\times$ 10-1.
The value of x is _______. (Rounded off to the nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: Cl 2 (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ 2Cl(g) Let moles of both of Cl 2 and Cl molecule be x. Partial pressure of Cl is, $p_{Cl}=\frac{x}{2x} \times 1=\frac{1}{2}$ Partial pressure of Cl 2 is, $p_{Cl_{2}}=\frac{x}{2x} \times 1=\frac{1}{2}$ Now, $K_{p}=\frac{(p_{Cl})^{2}}{p_{Cl_{2}}}$ $\Rightarrow K_{p}=\frac{(1/2)^{2}}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5$ = 5 $\times$ 10 $-$ 1 Hence, x $\times$ 10 $-$ 1 x = 5
questions.explanation_html:
Cl2(g) $\rightleftharpoons$ 2Cl(g)

Let moles of both of Cl2 and Cl molecule be x.

Partial pressure of Cl is, $p_{Cl}=\frac{x}{2x} \times 1=\frac{1}{2}$

Partial pressure of Cl2 is, $p_{Cl_{2}}=\frac{x}{2x} \times 1=\frac{1}{2}$

Now, $K_{p}=\frac{(p_{Cl})^{2}}{p_{Cl_{2}}}$

$\Rightarrow K_{p}=\frac{(1/2)^{2}}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5$

= 5 $\times$ 10 $-$ 1

Hence, x $\times$ 10 $-$ 1

x = 5

questions.explanation_text: To determine the correct relationship between the equilibrium constants $K_{C}$ and $K_{p}$ for the reaction: $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{N(s)}+\frac{3}{2}\text{H}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Fe(s)}+\text{NH}_{3}\text{(g)}$ First, consider the general relationship between $K_{C}$ and $K_{p}$ : $K_{p}=K_{C}(RT)^{\Delta n}$ where $\Delta n$ is the change in the number of moles of gas between the products and the reactants, $R$ is the ideal gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin. For the given reaction, calculate $\Delta n$ : Moles of gas in products: NH 3(g) = 1 mole Moles of gas in reactants: $\frac{3}{2}$ H 2(g) = 1.5 moles Therefore: $\Delta n=1-1.5=-0.5$ Substitute this value into the equation relating $K_{C}$ and $K_{p}$ : $K_{p}=K_{C}(RT)^{-0.5}$ Rearrange to express $K_{C}$ : $K_{C}=K_{p}(RT)^{0.5}$ Thus, the correct option is: Option A: $K_{C}=K_{p}(RT)^{1/2}$

First, consider the general relationship between $K_{C}$ and $K_{p}$ :

$K_{p}=K_{C}(RT)^{\Delta n}$

where $\Delta n$ is the change in the number of moles of gas between the products and the reactants, $R$ is the ideal gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin.

For the given reaction, calculate $\Delta n$ :

Moles of gas in products: NH3(g) = 1 mole

Moles of gas in reactants: $\frac{3}{2}$ H2(g) = 1.5 moles

Therefore:

$\Delta n=1-1.5=-0.5$

Substitute this value into the equation relating $K_{C}$ and $K_{p}$ :

$K_{p}=K_{C}(RT)^{-0.5}$

Rearrange to express $K_{C}$ :

$K_{C}=K_{p}(RT)^{0.5}$

Thus, the correct option is:

Option A: $K_{C}=K_{p}(RT)^{1/2}$

questions.question_text: If the equilibrium constant for A ⇌ B + C is $K_{eq}^{(1)}$ and that of B + C ⇌ P is $K_{eq}^{(2)}$ , the equilibrium constant for A ⇌ P is :
questions.question_html:
If the equilibrium constant for
A ⇌ B + C is $K_{eq}^{(1)}$ and that of
B + C ⇌ P is $K_{eq}^{(2)}$ , the equilibrium
constant for A ⇌ P is :
questions.explanation_text: We have two reactions: $A \rightleftharpoons B+C\text{with}K_{eq}^{(1)}$ $B+C \rightleftharpoons P\text{with}K_{eq}^{(2)}$ We want the equilibrium constant for the overall reaction $A \rightleftharpoons P.$ How to combine the equilibrium constants When two reactions are added to yield a net (overall) reaction, the equilibrium constant of the net reaction is the product of the equilibrium constants of the individual reactions . Formally: $\text{(Reaction 1)}+\text{(Reaction 2)} \Rightarrow \text{(Net Reaction)},$ and $K_{\text{net}}=K_{\text{(Reaction 1)}} \times K_{\text{(Reaction 2)}}.$ Applying it here Reaction 1 : $A \rightarrow B+C$ has $K_{eq}^{(1)}.$ Reaction 2 : $B+C \rightarrow P$ has $K_{eq}^{(2)}.$ When we add them, $\underset{\text{Reactant 1}}{\underset{⏟}{A}} \longrightarrow \underset{\text{Products of Reaction 1}=\text{Reactants of Reaction 2}}{\underset{}{B+C}} \longrightarrow \underset{\text{Product of Reaction 2}}{\underset{⏟}{P}}.$ So the net reaction is $A \rightarrow P$ , and its equilibrium constant is $K_{eq}^{\text{(net)}}=K_{eq}^{(1)} \times K_{eq}^{(2)}.$ Thus, the correct answer is: $K_{eq}^{(1)}K_{eq}^{(2)}.$ Hence, the answer (Option D) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
We have two reactions:

$A \rightleftharpoons B+C\text{with}K_{eq}^{(1)}$

$B+C \rightleftharpoons P\text{with}K_{eq}^{(2)}$

We want the equilibrium constant for the overall reaction

$A \rightleftharpoons P.$

How to combine the equilibrium constants

When two reactions are added to yield a net (overall) reaction, the equilibrium constant of the net reaction is the product of the equilibrium constants of the individual reactions. Formally:

$\text{(Reaction 1)}+\text{(Reaction 2)} \Rightarrow \text{(Net Reaction)},$

and

$K_{\text{net}}=K_{\text{(Reaction 1)}} \times K_{\text{(Reaction 2)}}.$

Applying it here

Reaction 1: $A \rightarrow B+C$ has $K_{eq}^{(1)}.$

Reaction 2: $B+C \rightarrow P$ has $K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

When we add them,

$\underset{\text{Reactant 1}}{\underset{⏟}{A}} \longrightarrow \underset{\text{Products of Reaction 1}=\text{Reactants of Reaction 2}}{\underset{}{B+C}} \longrightarrow \underset{\text{Product of Reaction 2}}{\underset{⏟}{P}}.$

So the net reaction is $A \rightarrow P$ , and its equilibrium constant is

$K_{eq}^{\text{(net)}}=K_{eq}^{(1)} \times K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

Thus, the correct answer is:

$K_{eq}^{(1)}K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

Hence, the answer (Option D) is correct.

questions.explanation_text: To determine the equilibrium constant, $K_{p}$ , for the decomposition reaction of the solid compound XY into its gaseous components X and Y, we need to consider the following reaction: $\text{XY (s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{X (g)}+\text{Y (g)}$ For a reaction where a solid decomposes into gases, the equilibrium constant $K_{p}$ is defined in terms of the partial pressures of the gaseous products. Since XY is a solid, its activity is considered to be 1 and does not appear in the equilibrium expression. Hence the expression for $K_{p}$ is: $K_{p}=P_{X} \cdot P_{Y}$ Where $P_{X}$ and $P_{Y}$ are the partial pressures of the gases X and Y, respectively. Given that the total pressure at equilibrium is 10 bar, and assuming that X and Y are present in equal amounts due to the stoichiometry of the decomposition reaction (i.e., 1:1), we can write: $P_{X}=P_{Y}=\frac{10}{2}=5\text{bar}$ Substituting these partial pressures into the expression for $K_{p}$ gives: $K_{p}=P_{X} \cdot P_{Y}=5\text{bar} \cdot 5\text{bar}=25\text{bar}^{2}$ Therefore, the equilibrium constant $K_{p}$ for this reaction is 25. $K_{p}=P_{X} \cdot P_{Y}$

Where $P_{X}$ and $P_{Y}$ are the partial pressures of the gases X and Y, respectively.
